scenes.tts: The answer is central. Roy and Cullen recorded vestibular-only neurons in four alert macaques, in vivo. These are neurons of the vestibular nuclei. They respond to head motion, but not to eye movements. The researchers varied conditions such as head restraint and neck torque, with magnetic search coils tracking head and gaze. Earlier work showed the afferents keep firing, so the cancellation is central.

scenes.tts: Now take made-up numbers. They are an illustration, not data. A passive turn peaks at twenty degrees per second. It evokes a modulation of forty spikes per second. Divide the modulation by the peak speed to get sensitivity. Here it is two point zero. An active turn of the same size evokes only four spikes per second. Sensitivity is zero point two. So the response is ninety percent cancelled.

scenes.tts: What lets the neuron cancel? In the neurons tested, cancelling the response to active motion required neck proprioceptive activation. That is feedback from the neck. And it had to match the feedback expected from the motor command. The command sets what the neck should report.
scenes.visual: Motor command gives expected feedback; neck proprioception gives actual feedback; both meet at a dashed match box; match leads to cancelled response

scenes.tts: Three limits matter. The comparator circuit was not located. Not every vestibular neuron was shown to cancel. And cancelling does not mean the periphery switched off, since the afferents kept firing. The recordings show what these neurons did. They suggest a role in neck reflex control. They do not explain how a turn feels. Cancellation is conditional, not automatic. Keep this rule. In the neurons tested, the cancelling is central, and it held only when neck feedback matched the expected feedback.
